screens.title: Control Structures, Functions, and Modifiers
screens.subtitle: Directing execution, shaping function behavior, and enforcing rules in Solidity

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to direct the flow of execution inside smart contracts, how to write functions with the right accessibility and behavior, and how to enforce rules with reusable modifiers. We start by mastering conditional statements so your contract can make decisions based on inputs or the caller, and then cover loops with a focus on gas costs so you can avoid common performance traps. Next you will learn how visibility and state mutability qualifiers—public, private, internal, external, view, pure, and payable—change who can call a function and whether it touches state or receives Ether. You will also build and apply function modifiers to centralize checks like ownership or input validation, and learn how to handle errors properly with require, revert, and assert. Throughout, concrete examples show the code patterns and common mistakes to avoid, and the hands-on vault activity ties these techniques together in a practical scenario. By the end you’ll be able to write functions that are secure, efficient, and clear about who can call them and whether they accept value.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Control flow, function design, and modifiers are the building blocks of secure, gas-aware Solidity contracts. They determine behavior, access, and error response.

content.html:

Modifiers & Errors

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to practical skills you'll practice in code. First, you will implement conditional logic using if, else if, and else statements to control when functions execute and to protect state changes. You should be able to read a boolean expression, trace which branch will run, and write a safe fallback branch that handles unexpected inputs. Second, you will understand for and while loops and when to avoid them inside transactions. That means recognizing gas limits and choosing pagination or off-chain work for large datasets. Third, you will define functions with visibility specifiers—public, private, internal, external—so you can expose or hide behavior correctly and avoid accidental access. Finally, you'll distinguish view and pure functions from payable ones and correctly allow Ether transfers in safe places. Each objective will combine definition, example, and a small mnemonic to help you recall when to use each pattern.

keyIdea.title: Core competencies
keyIdea.text: Write conditional checks, design gas-aware loops, choose correct visibility and mutability, and safely accept or reject Ether.

screens.title: Conditional Statements: if / else if / else
screens.subtitle: Declare decision points and protect state transitions

narration.text: A conditional statement is a decision point that evaluates a boolean expression to determine which block of code runs. In Solidity, if evaluates the first condition; else if offers secondary checks if the first was false; and else provides a fallback when none match. Use these constructs to gate sensitive operations such as administrative actions or state changes. For example, checking whether the caller equals an owner address before updating a value prevents unauthorized updates. A common misuse is leaving out a final else to handle unexpected inputs, which can silently skip crucial logic. Another mistake is performing expensive operations inside conditional branches without validating gas implications. Practice writing short, clear conditions and prefer explicit error messages with require when a branch must not continue. Concrete example: require(msg. sender == owner, "Not authorized") combined with an else that reverts ensures both clarity and state safety. Key takeaway: conditionals must be explicit and paired with clear error handling to avoid ambiguous contract states. Reflect: which state changes in your contract should never execute without an ownership or role check? Conditional Statements: if / else if / else means always validate critical conditions explicitly and provide clear failure messages so callers and tools can reason about outcomes.. In practical terms, declare decision points and protect state transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision safety
keyIdea.text: Always validate critical conditions explicitly and provide clear failure messages so callers and tools can reason about outcomes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Conditionals
Definition
if / else if / else
Evaluate boolean expressions so only eligible code paths run. Use require when a condition must hold before proceeding.
Example: require caller is owner before updating a protected variable.
Common mistake: relying on silent fall-through when a condition is false, leading to skipped state updates.
Key Takeaway

Write explicit checks and clear error messages so the contract state is always predictable after condition evaluation.

Concrete Example
// guard an action
if (msg.sender == owner) {
  value = _newValue;
} else {
  revert('Not authorized');
}
This pattern ensures only the owner can mutate state and provides a clear revert message when the check fails.
Check Your Understanding
What would happen if you omitted the revert and left the branch empty? Consider how the contract state and caller expectations change.

screens.title: Loops and Gas: for / while
screens.subtitle: Repeat with care — strategies to avoid gas exhaustion

narration.text: Loops let a contract perform repeated work, but every loop iteration consumes gas. In Solidity, for and while loops behave like in other languages: they repeat a block while a condition holds. The critical difference in blockchain code is that a transaction has a gas limit, and unbounded or large loops can exceed that limit and fail, wasting gas and creating bad user experiences. A concrete example from the chapter shows a function that sums elements up to a provided limit with a safety require ensuring the limit does not exceed the array length. That guard prevents out-of-bounds behavior, but it does not prevent running out of gas if the loop is large. A common solution is to design contracts so that you never loop over an unbounded dataset in a single transaction: implement pagination, let users claim results individually, or move heavy computation off-chain. Practice: when you see code iterating across an array, ask whether the array could grow without bounds. If it can, redesign. Misconception: loops are cheap because they run locally; they are not — every iteration is executed by miners and billed. Takeaway: prefer small, bounded loops and consider pull-based designs for large sets.

keyIdea.title: Bound loops or avoid them
keyIdea.text: Always ensure loop bounds are explicit and small, or shift work off-chain or to user-driven claims to avoid gas limit failures.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Loops & Gas
Definition
for and while
Repeat code blocks but remember each iteration costs gas. Always bound iterations or avoid them on large datasets.
Safety pattern: require the loop limit is less than or equal to the array length before iterating.
Misconception: looping off-chain is the same. On-chain loops still incur gas and can fail if large.
Code Example
function processNumbers(uint _limit) public view returns (uint sum) {
    require(_limit <= numbers.length, "Limit exceeds array size");
    for (uint i = 0; i < _limit; i++) {
      sum += numbers[i];
    }
    return sum;
}
This example enforces a limit, but still runs one iteration per item. For large arrays, prefer alternative designs such as pagination or pull-based claiming.
Try this
Identify a function in your code that iterates an array and ask whether that array is bounded. If not, sketch a pull-based alternative.

screens.title: Functions: Signatures, Parameters, and Returns
screens.subtitle: Encapsulate logic with clear inputs and outputs

narration.text: Functions are the named blocks of logic that perform actions or compute values inside a contract. A function signature includes its name, parameter list, visibility and mutability qualifiers, and return types. Parameters are the data a function expects; returns are what it hands back to the caller. For example, a simple add function takes two unsigned integers and returns their sum. When you design functions, keep them focused and small: a function should have a single responsibility and minimal side effects. Explicit return names can improve readability and tests. A common misconception is that public functions only matter for external callers; public also enables internal calls and sometimes adds gas overhead compared to external, so choose based on how the function will be used. Also prefer view and pure when state is not modified so callers can call them off-chain without spending gas. Practical habit: write a one-line comment describing what the function expects and what it guarantees before implementing it. Takeaway: clear signatures make your contract easier to reason about and safer to test. Functions: Signatures, Parameters, and Returns means small, well-typed functions with explicit parameters and returns improve security, testing, and reuse.. In practical terms, encapsulate logic with clear inputs and outputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design for clarity
keyIdea.text: Small, well-typed functions with explicit parameters and returns improve security, testing, and reuse.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Functions
Concept
Parameters & Returns
Clearly typed inputs and outputs establish expectations for callers and tests. Use return names for readability.
Example: function add(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint sum) { sum = a + b; }
Misconception: public is always best. If a function is only meant for external callers, external may be more efficient for complex types.
Concrete Example
function add(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint sum) {
  sum = a + b;
}
This pure function does not read or write contract state and can be invoked without a transaction when called off-chain.
Key Takeaway
Keep signatures explicit so callers and tests know exactly what the function expects and returns.

screens.title: Visibility Specifiers: public / private / internal / external
screens.subtitle: Who can call this function, and from where?

narration.text: Visibility specifiers control who can call a function and where. Public functions are the most open: they can be called externally by users and other contracts, as well as internally by the contract's own functions. Private functions are the most restrictive and are callable only within the same contract; they are not visible to inheriting contracts. Internal functions are like private but also available to derived contracts that inherit from the current contract. External functions are callable only from outside the contract; they cannot be called internally using a simple internal call, and they can be more gas-efficient for external inputs because parameters use calldata. A common misconception is that public and external are interchangeable. Choose external when you expect only external callers and you want to avoid unnecessary memory copies for large arrays or structs. Choose internal for helper logic that derived contracts should use, and private for implementation details that must remain internal to the contract. Example: an external getter for an A P I-like call, an internal helper to update state, and a private utility for sensitive arithmetic. Takeaway: visibility is both a security and gas design decision—pick the narrowest scope that still supports needed behavior.

keyIdea.title: Minimize exposure
keyIdea.text: Apply the narrowest visibility that still meets your functional needs to reduce attack surface and unnecessary gas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Visibility
Public vs External
Public
Callable both externally and internally. Use when internal calls are needed.
External
Callable only from outside the contract; often more gas-efficient for external-only interfaces.
Private vs Internal
Private
Only callable within the same contract; not visible to inheriting contracts.
Internal
Callable within the contract and by derived contracts; useful for reusable helpers.
Example Decision
If a function exists only to provide an API for users, prefer external; if it is a helper for derived contracts, prefer internal.

screens.title: State Mutability: view, pure, and payable
screens.subtitle: Declare intent about state reads, writes, and Ether transfers

narration.text: State mutability specifiers describe how a function interacts with contract state and value. A view function reads state but must not modify it, making it safe to call off-chain without spending gas. A pure function neither reads nor modifies state and depends only on its inputs; it is ideal for deterministic utility computations. Payable marks a function as able to receive Ether with a transaction. If a function is not payable and Ether is sent to it, the transaction reverts — a critical safety mechanism to avoid accidental Ether loss. Use view and pure where possible to make intent explicit and to allow callers and tooling to avoid unnecessary transactions. A common misconception is that view or pure guarantees zero cost; while they are free when called locally, calling them from a transaction still consumes gas. Practical example: a multiply function that returns the product of two inputs is pure; a balance getter is view; a deposit function that needs to accept Ether must be payable and validate msg. value. Takeaway: choose the narrowest mutability that expresses what your function really does.

keyIdea.title: Declare intent
keyIdea.text: Use view and pure for read-only or input-only computations, and payable only when the function should accept Ether.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Mutability
What they mean
view · pure · payable
Use view for read-only state access; pure for functions that only use inputs; and payable when the function must accept Ether with the call. Validate msg.value when taking Ether.
Example: function multiply(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint) { return a * b; }
Example: function deposit() public payable { /* msg.value contains the Ether sent */ }
Quick Check
If a function does not touch state and returns a value computed only from inputs, mark it pure. If it reads state but doesn't change it, mark it view.

screens.title: Payable Functions and Ether Handling
screens.subtitle: Accept value intentionally and validate amounts

narration.text: A payable function is the only kind that can accept Ether as part of the transaction. If you send Ether to a non-payable function, the transaction will revert. Inside a payable function, the special variable that contains the sent amount is available so you can validate or record it. For example, a deposit function could read the received amount and update a balance mapping. Be explicit about who may call payable functions; in many contracts only the owner or specific addresses should be allowed to trigger Ether-receiving logic. The chapter example uses a deposit function declared public payable and notes that msg. value contains the amount sent. A common pitfall is failing to check msg. value or forgetting to mark the function payable, causing accidental reverts. Another risk is allowing anyone to send Ether to functions that modify sensitive state without proper checks. Takeaway: mark Ether-accepting functions as payable and validate amounts and caller permissions before changing state. How would you limit deposits to the owner while still allowing authorized withdrawers to pull funds later? Payable Functions and Ether Handling means only mark functions payable when they should accept value, and always validate msg.value and caller permissions.. In practical terms, accept value intentionally and validate amounts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Accept Ether intentionally
keyIdea.text: Only mark functions payable when they should accept value, and always validate msg.value and caller permissions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Payable
Concept
public payable
A payable function receives Ether via the transaction. Use msg.value to inspect the amount and update balances only after validation.
function deposit() public payable {
  // msg.value is the Ether sent
  // update balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
}
Common pitfall
If not marked payable, any Ether sent reverts. If unchecked, malicious actors could force unexpected state changes with value-bearing calls.

screens.title: Function Modifiers
screens.subtitle: Reusable pre- and post-conditions like onlyOwner

narration.text: Function modifiers let you apply reusable checks or behavior around function execution. A modifier defines logic and uses the placeholder that indicates where the modified function's body should run. Common modifiers include ownership checks and input validation. For example, an onlyOwner modifier checks that the caller is the contract deployer and then yields to the function body. Modifiers reduce duplication and centralize policy so every function guarded by the modifier has consistent behavior. You can stack modifiers in a function signature so several checks run in sequence. Misconception: modifiers are purely syntactic sugar; while they are convenient, they also affect gas and call flow, so keep them minimal and clear. The chapter demonstrates both onlyOwner and greaterThanZero modifiers applied to a setValue function. When writing modifiers, put the most restrictive or cheapest checks first to fail fast and minimize gas wasted on additional checks. Takeaway: use modifiers to express access and validation rules clearly and consistently across functions. Function Modifiers means modifiers centralize repeated validation logic, improving readability and reducing the surface for copy-paste mistakes.. In practical terms, reusable pre- and post-conditions like onlyowner. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Centralize checks
keyIdea.text: Modifiers centralize repeated validation logic, improving readability and reducing the surface for copy-paste mistakes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Modifiers
Syntax
modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, 'Caller is not the owner'); _; }
The underscore indicates where the modified function's code will execute. Modifiers can be stacked to run multiple checks in order.
Applied Example
modifier greaterThanZero(uint _amount) {
  require(_amount > 0, 'Amount must be greater than zero');
  _;
}

function setValue(uint256 _newValue) public onlyOwner greaterThanZero(_newValue) {
  value = _newValue;
}
Stacking enforces owner and amount checks before the state change. Place fast, cheap checks first to fail early.

screens.title: Error Handling: require, revert, and assert
screens.subtitle: Choose the right mechanism for expected and invariant failures

narration.text: Solidity offers three primary mechanisms for stopping execution and reverting state when something goes wrong. Require is used for input validation and expected preconditions; it reverts the transaction and refunds unused gas when the condition is false and can include a helpful error message. Revert is equivalent in effect and is useful when you want to stop execution after evaluating a more complex condition or sequence of checks. Assert is intended for internal consistency checks that should never fail; if an assert fails it indicates a serious bug, and it consumes all remaining gas. Use require and revert for expected user errors such as invalid inputs or insufficient balance, and reserve assert for invariants that represent internal contract correctness. A concrete example shows require used to ensure a loop limit does not exceed an array size and to validate amounts in withdraw functions. A common error is to overuse assert for input validation, which can make failures more costly and less informative. Takeaway: pick require or revert for recoverable or expected errors with messages, and use assert only for invariants that indicate a broken contract assumption.

keyIdea.title: Fail intentionally
keyIdea.text: Use require/revert for user-facing validations and assert only for conditions that should never happen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Error Handling
require
Validate inputs and expected conditions early. If the check fails, revert and return unused gas.
Example: require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, 'Insufficient balance');
revert · assert
Use revert for complex conditional exits; use assert only for invariants. If assert fails, it signals a critical bug and consumes all gas.
Misuse: using assert for normal input validation can make ordinary errors costly and opaque.
Key Takeaway

Choose require/revert for expected checks with messages and assert only for never-fail invariants.

screens.title: Walkthrough: FunctionAndControl Contract
screens.subtitle: Inspect visibility, modifiers, loops, and assertions in a single example

narration.text: Let's walk through a compact contract that demonstrates many chapter ideas together. The contract declares an owner, a protected value, and a private numbers array. It defines modifiers such as onlyOwner to centralize ownership checks and greaterThanZero to validate amounts. Functions include public setValue guarded by both modifiers, an external getValue marked view to return state without modifying it, internal and private helpers that change value internally, and a pure multiply function that performs computation without touching state. The processNumbers function shows a safe loop pattern: it requires the provided limit to be within the array bounds before summing elements. Lastly, the checkInvariant function uses assert to ensure a divisor is never zero. As you read the code, identify where visibility prevents external calls, how modifiers reduce duplication, and where mutability clarifies intent. Common misconception: seeing internal and private functions and assuming they are equivalent—remember internal is visible to derived contracts while private is not. Takeaway: study this contract to see how small, focused functions, clear modifiers, and guarded loops combine to produce readable and safer logic. Walkthrough: FunctionAndControl Contract means a single contract can show visibility, mutability, modifiers, safe loops, and error handling working together to enforce rules clearly.. In practical terms, inspect visibility, modifiers, loops, and assertions in a single example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Integrated example
keyIdea.text: A single contract can show visibility, mutability, modifiers, safe loops, and error handling working together to enforce rules clearly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Contract Walkthrough
Excerpt
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract FunctionAndControl {
    address public owner;
    uint256 public value = 100;
    uint256[] private numbers;

    modifier onlyOwner() {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Caller is not the owner");
        _;
    }

    modifier greaterThanZero(uint _amount) {
        require(_amount > 0, "Amount must be greater than zero");
        _;
    }

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
        numbers.push(10);
        numbers.push(20);
        numbers.push(30);
    }

    function setValue(uint256 _newValue) public onlyOwner greaterThanZero(_newValue) {
        require(_newValue <= 1000, "Value cannot exceed 1000");
        value = _newValue;
    }
}
Highlights
  • Modifiers: onlyOwner centralizes access control.
  • Visibility: owner is public; numbers is private to prevent direct external reads.
  • Safety: require guards inputs and loop limits.
  • Mutability: setValue is non-view because it updates state; multiply is pure elsewhere.
Reflection
Which checks catch invalid inputs, and which checks guard internal invariants? Separate those concerns in your designs.

screens.title: Build: AccessControlledVault.sol
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step plan to implement the restricted vault

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to create a vault where only the owner can deposit Ether and only authorized addresses can withdraw limited amounts. Start by declaring an owner state variable and a mapping from address to bool that records authorized withdrawers. Implement an onlyOwner modifier that checks msg. sender equals owner and use it to protect the deposit and authorization function. The deposit function must be public and payable and should validate that only the owner may call it. The authorizeWithdrawers function should be public, use onlyOwner, and set the mapping for a given user. The withdraw function should check that the caller is authorized, that the requested amount is positive, and that the contract has a sufficient balance. It should also ensure the amount does not exceed a per-withdraw limit, for example one ether, using require checks with clear messages. For sending Ether the chapter suggests using the send pattern used in the exercise; follow the provided guidance. As you implement, test the contract by simulating owner and authorized withdrawer roles and try edge cases like withdrawing more than the balance. Takeaway: focus on clear role checks, explicit value validation, and bounded withdrawals to reduce risk.

keyIdea.title: Activity blueprint
keyIdea.text: Design the vault with owner-only deposits, a mapping for authorized withdrawers, and bounded withdraw checks to limit exposure.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Vault Activity
Plan
  1. Declare owner and mapping(address => bool) authorizedWithdrawers.
  2. Write onlyOwner modifier and constructor to set owner.
  3. Implement public payable deposit() protected by onlyOwner and checking msg.value as needed.
  4. Implement authorizeWithdrawers(address _user, bool _status) with onlyOwner.
  5. Implement withdraw(uint256 _amount) that checks authorization, amount bounds, and contract balance.
Starter Skeleton
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract AccessControlledVault {
    address public owner;
    mapping(address => bool) public authorizedWithdrawers;

    modifier onlyOwner() {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Not the owner");
        _;
    }

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
    }

    // TODO: deposit(), authorizeWithdrawers(), withdraw()
}
Test edge cases: non-owner deposit attempts, withdraw amount zero, amount exceeding balance, and multiple authorized accounts.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid gas traps, unclear visibility, and weak error handling

narration.text: This final lesson on implementation concerns highlights recurring mistakes and practical best practices. First, avoid unbounded loops that can run out of gas; when you need to process large datasets, prefer pagination, pull-based claiming, or off-chain computations. Second, choose the narrowest visibility necessary—exposing internal helpers as public increases attack surface and may introduce unexpected call paths. Third, consistently use require and revert for expected validation with descriptive messages; reserve assert for invariants that indicate internal bugs. Fourth, validate Ether transfers and declare payable only for functions that should accept value. Fifth, keep modifiers simple and fail-fast: put cheap checks like ownership verification before more expensive operations. A common pitfall is stacking many expensive operations after a costly check; instead, validate first and then run heavier logic. For testing, include unit tests that simulate owner, unauthorized, and boundary conditions to confirm your checks. Takeaway: design for minimal privilege, explicit validation, and gas-awareness so your contracts remain secure and predictable in real deployments. Common Mistakes and Best Practices means minimize privileges, validate early, prefer bounded work, and write tests covering owner, unauthorized, and boundary cases.. In practical terms, avoid gas traps, unclear visibility, and weak error handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Secure-by-design
keyIdea.text: Minimize privileges, validate early, prefer bounded work, and write tests covering owner, unauthorized, and boundary cases.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Best Practices
Avoid these common mistakes
  • Unbounded loops: Can cause out-of-gas failures; redesign long iterations into smaller operations.
  • Overexposed visibility: Public where internal or private is intended increases risk.
  • Misused assert: Use it only for invariants, not for normal input validation.
  • Missing payable: Forgetting payable on functions that receive Ether will cause reverts.
Action Items
Write unit tests for owner and unauthorized flows.
Prefer fail-fast require checks with messages.
Limit loop size and avoid state-changing mass-ops in one transaction.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas to carry forward

narration.text: These three concepts summarize the practical core of the chapter. First, conditional statements let you make decisions and must be paired with clear error handling to protect state. Second, loops are powerful but expensive; always ensure they are bounded, or use alternative designs like pagination or off-chain computation. Third, function visibility and mutability communicate who can call a function and whether it touches state or accepts Ether—pick the narrowest option that meets your requirements. Keep these ideas in mind as you design and review contracts: predictable decision logic, gas-awareness in repeated work, and explicit function contracts make safe, maintainable code. Key Concepts — Part 1 means decisions, bounded repetition, and explicit function intent form the foundation of safe solidity development.. In practical terms, three essential ideas to carry forward. narration.text: Here are three more compact reminders. Use modifiers to centralize access checks like onlyOwner, which reduces duplication and keeps logic consistent. Prefer require and revert for expected validation with readable messages, and reserve assert for internal invariants that should never fail. Finally, apply practical patterns: protect deposits with payable and msg. value checks, bound withdrawals and loop iterations, and write unit tests that exercise owner, unauthorized, and edge-case behavior. These practices keep contracts maintainable and robust under real network conditions.
